title: Real ROI: Lessons from Enterprises that have already succeeded with LLMs at Scale: Raza Habib

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is about operating LLM systems in production at scale, covering LLMOps practices including evaluation, logging, trace replay, quality monitoring, and regression testing across hundreds of companies. The talk draws cross-industry lessons from legal, education, compliance, and developer-tool companies without focusing on a single vertical. The speaker explicitly advocates embedding evaluation at every stage from lightweight prototyping through production monitoring and regression testing. The content assumes working knowledge of LLMs and production systems but is pitched at practicing engineers and product leaders. Recorded live conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. All twelve evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with specific character ranges and excerpts.

summary: Raza Habib, CEO and cofounder of Humanloop—one of the first LLM Ops platforms—shares practical lessons from enterprises that have achieved real ROI with LLMs at scale. Having helped hundreds of companies get AI into production, Habib stresses the industry has moved past experimentation into generating real revenue and cost savings. Filevine, a legal tech company in a regulated industry, launched six products in a year and roughly doubled its revenue. Habib simplifies LLM applications into four chained components: a base model, a prompt template, a data selection strategy (e.g., RAG or API), and function calling. He cites GitHub Copilot as the first commercially successful LLM app, using this structure with a fine-tuned model and context-aware code suggestions from the last ten files a user touched. He predicts application complexity will decrease as models improve. He frames success around three fundamentals—people, ideas, and machines—borrowing from Boyd's dictum. Successful teams need less ML expertise than expected: primarily generalist full-stack product engineers and domain experts. Domain experts are the most important and underappreciated members—Duolingo's linguists do all prompt engineering; Filevine's legal professionals write prompts that become production code; Fathom's PM crafts context-specific meeting summaries. Evaluation must be central from the start, as the combinatorial space of decisions is too large to navigate by eyeballing outputs. Best companies embed evaluation at every stage: lightweight during prototyping, monitoring in production, and regression testing for prompt or model changes. End user feedback is the ground truth for subjective tasks—GitHub Copilot tracks suggestion acceptance and code persistence at intervals—but it is lower volume and unavailable during development. Teams supplement with LLM-as-judge scorecards, breaking subjective criteria into specific, independently scorable binary questions rather than asking for a single judgment. Traditional code-based metrics (precision, recall, latency) remain, and human evaluation cannot be fully eliminated. Optimization follows a Pareto frontier of trade-offs rather than a single God metric. On tooling, three fundamentals emerge: systems must optimize team collaboration so domain experts can participate in prompts and evaluation, support evaluation at every stage, and provide comprehensive logging with replay capability. Ironclad nearly abandoned agents before building logging and rerunning infrastructure (Rivet, now open source), after which they achieved production performance auto-negotiating roughly 50% of contracts for their largest customers. Notion and Filevine similarly rely on comprehensive logging and prompt management systems to enable domain experts, data scientists, and PMs to collaborate effectively.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Real ROI Message
sections.summary: Raza Habib introduces himself as CEO of Humanloop, one of the first LLM Ops platforms, which has helped hundreds of companies. He emphasizes the industry has moved past experimentation to real revenue and cost savings, citing Filevine which launched six products and roughly doubled revenue in the past year.

sections.title: Four Components of LLM Applications
sections.summary: Habib simplifies LLM applications into four chained components: base model, prompt template, data selection strategy, and function calling. He uses GitHub Copilot as a concrete example with a fine-tuned model and context-aware code suggestions. He predicts application complexity will decrease as models improve, arguing current chaining is a workaround for model limitations.

sections.title: Three Fundamentals and Team Composition
sections.summary: Borrowing Boyd's 'people, ideas, machines' framework, Habib identifies three fundamentals: right people, clear evaluation criteria, and proper tooling. Successful teams need less ML expertise than expected—primarily generalist full-stack engineers and domain experts, with modest data science knowledge. Domain experts are the most important and underappreciated members.

sections.title: Domain Expert Examples
sections.summary: Habib illustrates domain expertise importance with examples: Duolingo linguists do all prompt engineering; Filevine legal professionals write prompts that become production code; Ironclad involves legal expertise; Fathom's PM crafts context-specific meeting summaries for different user types.

sections.title: Evaluation as Baseline Core
sections.summary: Habib stresses baseline evaluation must be central from the start. The combinatorial space of decisions across model, data selection, prompt templates, and tools is too large to navigate without a proper evaluation strategy. Teams without one spin their wheels making changes and eyeballing outputs.

sections.title: Evaluation at Every Stage and End User Feedback
sections.summary: Best companies embed evaluation at every development stage in different forms: lightweight during prototyping, monitoring in production, and regression testing for prompt or model changes. End user feedback is the ground truth for subjective tasks—GitHub Copilot tracks suggestion acceptance and code persistence at intervals—but is lower volume and unavailable during development. Four feedback types are collected: actions, issues, direct votes, and corrections, with user edits being especially rich signal.

sections.title: LLM as Judge and Metric Scoreboards
sections.summary: Teams build scorecards of different evaluator types. LLM-as-judge works well when subjective criteria are broken into specific, independently scorable binary questions rather than ambiguous single judgments. Ordering biases must be managed. Traditional code-based metrics (precision, recall, latency) remain, and human evaluation cannot be fully eliminated. Optimization follows a Pareto frontier of trade-offs, not a single God metric, because product experience quality is multifaceted. Hex breaks evaluations into binary pieces; Vanta uses automated evaluation mixed with human feedback in a regulated, high-stakes context.

sections.title: Tooling Fundamentals and Company Examples
sections.summary: Three tooling fundamentals: optimize team collaboration so domain experts can participate in prompts and evaluation, support evaluation at every stage, and provide comprehensive logging with replay capability. Ironclad nearly abandoned agents before building Rivet (open source logging and rerunning tool), after which they achieved production performance auto-negotiating roughly 50% of contracts for largest customers. Notion relies on detailed logging to replay production runs. Filevine uses Humanloop as system of record for prompts where legal professionals collaborate with data scientists and PMs.
